title: Structuring & Documenting a Submission
summary: What a take-home repo needs beyond working code, since evaluators usually review it without you there to explain any of it.

slides.markdown:
Once you build knowing what to prioritize (see [take-home-strategy](take-home-strategy)), the next failure mode is different: code that works perfectly on your machine but reads as confusing or incomplete to someone who never watched you build it.

A take-home is usually reviewed **asynchronously** — no you in the room to explain a weird decision or walk through setup. That means the README, tests, and project layout have to do the explaining your voice would normally do. This topic covers structuring a submission so it explains itself: what the README needs to carry, what tests to include on a time budget, and how to write a trade-offs section that turns missing scope into a strength.

slides.sectionTitle: The README as your only chance to narrate decisions
slides.markdown:
In a live interview, you narrate your thinking as you go. In a take-home, the README is the entire substitute for that narration — it's frequently the *first* thing a reviewer opens, and for a skim-level review it might be the *only* thing they read closely.

A strong README answers, in this rough order: how to run it, what it does, the key design decisions and why, what you explicitly deferred, and how you tested it. Skipping the "why" and only describing "what" wastes the README's real purpose — a reviewer can see the *what* by reading the code; they can't see your reasoning without you writing it down.

Treat the README as a **cover letter for the code**, not an afterthought bolted on at the end.

slides.sectionTitle: What tests to include given the time budget
slides.markdown:
You almost never have time for exhaustive coverage, so testing on a take-home is itself a prioritization exercise. Spend your limited test-writing time on the **riskiest paths**: the trickiest business logic, boundary conditions the prompt hints at (empty input, duplicate entries, a negative number where one shouldn't appear), and anything you're least confident is correct.

Skip exhaustive tests for straightforward code — a getter, a simple mapping function — where a bug would be obvious on the first manual run anyway. A handful of sharp, well-chosen tests around the risky logic reads as stronger judgment than fifty tests that mostly assert trivial things.

If you genuinely ran out of time for tests, say so in the README with what you'd add — that's a better signal than silence or than tests written in the last five minutes that don't actually assert anything meaningful.

slides.sectionTitle: Writing a trade-offs section: what you'd do with more time
slides.markdown:
A dedicated "trade-offs" or "what I'd do with more time" section in the README is one of the highest-leverage things you can write, because it directly answers the question every evaluator is silently asking: does this candidate know what's missing, or did they just stop?

Be specific rather than generic — "I'd add more tests" says nothing; "I'd add tests for concurrent writes to the same record, since the current implementation doesn't handle that race" shows you found a real gap and can reason about it precisely. List two or three concrete items, ranked by what you'd tackle first, rather than an exhaustive laundry list that dilutes the signal.

This section is also where you can flag a shortcut you know is fragile — for example, an in-memory store standing in for a real database — so the reviewer knows it was a deliberate scoping choice, not an oversight.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a minimal but complete project layout
slides.markdown:
A submission doesn't need elaborate architecture, but a predictable layout signals you'd fit into a real codebase. A minimal, complete shape for a small backend exercise:

```
.
├── README.md
├── src/
│   ├── api/          # route handlers
│   ├── models/       # data shapes
│   └── services/     # business logic
├── tests/
│   └── services/     # tests next to what they cover
├── package.json      # or requirements.txt / go.mod
└── .env.example      # config keys with placeholder values, never real secrets
```

The key signals here: tests mirror the source layout (a reviewer can find the test for a service without hunting), `.env.example` shows what config exists without leaking anything real, and there's no dead scaffolding — no empty `utils/` folder or unused `docker-compose.yml` left over from a template.

Before anything else, a reviewer needs to actually get your code running — and if that fails in the first two minutes, nothing else about your submission matters, because they can't observe it. Pin exact versions where they matter (a `package.json` engines field, a `.python-version` file), include a single command that installs dependencies and runs the app, and never assume a global tool is already installed on the reviewer's machine.

Test the runnability yourself in a genuinely clean environment right before submitting — a fresh clone into an empty directory, not the one you've been developing in, which likely has stray global installs or cached state masking a missing step.

If setup genuinely requires an external service (a database, an API key), provide a mock or an in-memory fallback so the reviewer isn't blocked waiting on infrastructure they don't have.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a bare code dump vs a documented submission on the same problem
slides.markdown:
The same solution can score very differently depending purely on how it's packaged.

| | Bare code dump | Documented submission |
|---|---|---|
| First impression | Reviewer has to reverse-engineer intent from code alone | README frames the approach before they read a line of code |
| Setup | "Figure it out" or missing entirely | One command, tested in a clean environment |
| Missing scope | Invisible until the reviewer notices a gap themselves | Named explicitly in a trade-offs section |
| Tests | Either absent or scattered with no clear intent | Concentrated on the riskiest logic, easy to find |
| Evaluator's read | "Can this person code?" — unknown beyond that | "Can this person code, communicate, and prioritize?" |

**How to decide:** given equal coding time, spending the last 20-30% of your budget on documentation and structure almost always raises your score more than spending it on one more feature.

slides.markdown:
![Timeline of a reviewer's 20-minute review](assets/review-time-breakdown.svg)

The practical implication: if setup fails at minute 5, the remaining 15 minutes of review either don't happen or happen in a much less charitable mood. Every minute you spend making the first two gates frictionless protects the value of everything you built after that.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: no setup instructions, so the evaluator can't even run it
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The code is self-explanatory, and any engineer can figure out how to run a project like this."

**Why it's wrong:** "figuring it out" costs the reviewer time they don't have in a 20-minute skim, and every minute spent debugging your environment setup is a minute not spent appreciating the actual solution. Worse, if setup fails outright — a missing dependency, an undocumented required environment variable — some reviewers will stop entirely and score what they can see, which is nothing.

**Correct model:** assume zero context. Write the exact commands to install, configure, and run the project, state any prerequisite (a specific runtime version, a service that must be running), and verify those steps yourself from a clean checkout before you submit.

slides.sectionTitle: Documenting decisions like a design doc, not a diary
slides.markdown:
There's a version of "documenting your decisions" that reads like a diary — a stream-of-consciousness account of what you tried and when. That's weaker than a design-doc style write-up: state the decision, the alternative you considered, and why you picked one over the other, in that order, without the narrative of your afternoon.

This mirrors the same skill covered in [writing-design-docs](writing-design-docs) for real engineering work — a take-home README is a miniature version of exactly that document, and reviewers who write design docs professionally will recognize the difference immediately.

Keep each decision to two or three sentences. A README that takes five minutes to read carries more signal than one that takes fifteen, because it forces you to identify which decisions were actually worth mentioning.

slides.sectionTitle: The senior-level nuance: writing for the reviewer who disagrees with you
slides.markdown:
A junior submission documents decisions assuming the reader will simply accept them. A senior one anticipates the reviewer who'd make a different choice, and pre-empts the objection: "I used an in-memory map instead of a real cache here — for this dataset size the added infra wasn't worth the setup time, but I'd swap to Redis before this saw real traffic."

That single sentence does three things at once: shows you know the limitation, shows you can justify a choice under constraints, and shows you know what the *right* long-term answer is. It's the same instinct that shows up in real design reviews — anticipating pushback and addressing it before it's raised, rather than being surprised by it later.

This is usually what separates a submission that reads as "correct" from one that reads as "ready for a senior role."
